newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Gorbachev unveils 'Earth Charter' at Rio +5 meeting.
newsitem.headline: Gorbachev unveils 'Earth Charter' at Rio +5 meeting.

text.p: Former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev on Tuesday unveiled a draft of the Rio +5 environmental meeting's "Earth Charter," which promotes environmentally friendly behaviour at every level of society.
The first draft of the so-called Earth Charter lists a set of 18 basic principles, based on issues ranging from sustainable development to justice, non-violence and gender equality.
It will be presented to heads of state in June when they meet at the United Nations in New York to carry out their reappraisal of the pledges made at the 1992 Earth Summit.

The weeklong Rio +5 conference, which ends on Thursday, has brought together hundreds of environmentalists, business men and United Nations officials to review and revive the pledges made at the 1992 Earth Summit, which was also held in Rio de Janeiro.
Rio +5 organisers and participants agree that governments have made little progress on implementing the environmental commitments they made in 1992 and that the issues were as pressing as ever.

"We have to abandon the stereotype of waiting for goverments to act, for U.N. committees to act," said Gorbachev, who is attending Rio +5 as president of Green Cross International. "We are orchestrating democratic pressure on those organisations which have to take action."
He said the Earth Charter was there to make people aware of environmental issues and give new impetus to civil society in its efforts to seek solutions and force governments to act.

Maurice Strong, president of the Earth Council non-governmental organisation, a driving force behind the Earth Summit and Rio +5, said the Earth Charter was aimed at stimulating debate and action within civil society.

"We are launching a worldwide process, moving literally tens of thousands of grass roots and non-governmental organisations, precisely to ensure that this does not remain just a bunch of nice words," Strong said.

He said contributions and support from people throughout the whole world would give the document its authority. The final text of the Earth Charter is to be presented for endorsement by the United Nations in the year 2000.
"This document will stand on its own authority," Strong said. "It will not depend on governments to assess it for its authority."
Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso addressed the conference on Tuesday, saying, "It is not just a challenge for governments, but a challenge for the whole of humanity."

World Bank President James Wolfensohn also addressed the meeting on Tuesday, saying the bank had committed mistakes in its development projects in the past but was now a reformed institution with a more human approach.

"The World Bank is now a very different institution, being less arrogant and listening more," Wolfensohn said. "There is a change in the approach of the bank in trying to give greater weight to social, cultural and human issues alongside economic issues, in terms of finance."
